videos.title: DNA replication – 3D
summary: DNA = two complementary, antiparallel strands (A–T, C–G), each with a 5′ and 3′ end.
Helicase unzips the helix → replication fork; each strand becomes a template.
Primase lays down a short RNA primer; DNA polymerase extends it, only 5′→3′.
Leading strand is made continuously; lagging strand is made in short Okazaki fragments, each starting from its own primer.
Exonuclease removes RNA primers, another DNA polymerase fills the gaps, DNA ligase seals the nicks.
Result is semi-conservative: each daughter helix = one old strand + one new strand.

videos.title: DNA Replication
summary: Bacterial replication shown in three phases: initiation, elongation, termination.
Initiation: DNA opens at the origin; a hexameric helicase is loaded on each side → two forks moving apart (replication bubble).
DNA polymerase cannot start from scratch – primase makes an RNA primer first.
Clamp loader uses ATP to open the ring-shaped sliding clamp around the primer–template junction; the clamp keeps the polymerase on the DNA (processivity).
Leading strand synthesised continuously; lagging strand primed repeatedly and made as Okazaki fragments, all 5′→3′.
Primers are later replaced with DNA and fragments joined by ligase.

videos.title: DNA animation (2002–2014) by Drew Berry & Etsuko Uno
summary: Compilation of WEHI molecular animations (no narration; on-screen text). The slide's link starts at 3:21 (its translation section).
Translation: mRNA threads through the ribosome; tRNAs bring amino acids matched codon-to-anticodon, and the polypeptide grows as each codon is read 5′→3′.
Earlier parts of the reel show DNA packaging (nucleosomes → chromosomes), replication and transcription – useful revision of the central dogma.

videos.title: DNA sequencing explained
summary: Sanger (capillary) sequencing: PCR-like reaction with normal dNTPs + a few fluorescent chain-terminating nucleotides (ddNTPs), one colour per base.
Whenever a terminator is incorporated, polymerase stops → products of every length, each ending in a coloured base.
Capillary electrophoresis separates fragments by size; DNA (negative) moves to + electrode, shorter fragments faster – single-nucleotide resolution.
A laser excites each fragment's dye at the end of the capillary; a camera records colour → chromatogram.
Reading the colour peaks in order of size gives the sequence, stored digitally for bioinformatics.

videos.title: H-Ras: active (GTP) → inactive (GDP) conformational change
summary: 10-second morph of the Ras protein structure between its GTP-bound (active) and GDP-bound (inactive) shapes.
Most of the protein is unchanged; the change is concentrated in the small 'switch' loops around the nucleotide (γ-phosphate senses GTP vs GDP).
GEF swaps GDP→GTP (turns ON); GAP stimulates GTP hydrolysis (turns OFF) – same switch logic used by motor proteins and G proteins.
Key point: a small chemical change (loss of one phosphate) → a conformational change that alters what the protein binds.

videos.title: Actin filament assembly
summary: F-actin filaments are built from G-actin monomers bound to ATP or ADP.
ATP-actin adds mainly at the barbed (+) end → elongation; ATP is hydrolysed to ADP after incorporation.
ADP-actin dissociates preferentially from the pointed (−) end.
Net addition at + and loss at − gives treadmilling; assembly is driven by ATP hydrolysis and nucleation can occur spontaneously in vitro.
Context for the slide: these polarised actin tracks are what myosin walks on in muscle.

videos.title: Muscle Myosin
summary: Myosin II is a dimer: two independent heads (catalytic core + lever arm) joined by a coiled-coil rod anchored in the thick filament.
Start: head holds ADP + Pi and binds actin weakly.
Head docks on actin → Pi released → strong binding + power stroke (lever arm swings, actin moves).
ADP leaves; ATP binds → head detaches from actin.
ATP hydrolysed on the detached head → lever re-cocks (stores energy like a spring); cycle repeats.
Actin doesn't slip back because many other myosin heads are attached at any moment.

videos.title: Bacterial flagellum
summary: Flagellum = helical filament (~20 nm wide, up to 15 µm long, ~100 rotations/s) + flexible hook + basal body.
Basal body: rod + rings in inner membrane, peptidoglycan and outer membrane (L and P rings in Gram-negatives act as a bearing).
Motor = stator (MotA/MotB, fixed to peptidoglycan) + rotor (FliG, FliM, FliN on the MS ring made of 26 FliF subunits).
Powered by a proton gradient (not ATP): H⁺ flow through MotA/MotB; a conserved Asp in MotB binds protons → conformational changes → power strokes on the rotor.
Assembly is inside-out: MS ring → rotor → export apparatus → rod → hook (with cap) → filament, with subunits exported through the hollow core and added at the distal tip.

videos.title: What is Apoptosis? The Apoptotic Pathways and the Caspase Cascade
summary: Apoptosis = programmed cell death; e.g. removes webbing between fetal fingers and eliminates cells with irreparable DNA damage.
Executed from within by caspases, which must first be activated.
Extrinsic pathway: FasL on a T cell binds Fas (death receptor) on the target → FADD adaptor → caspase cascade.
Intrinsic pathway: balance of anti-apoptotic Bcl-2/Bcl-xL vs pro-apoptotic Bax/Bak at mitochondria. Damage/loss of survival signals → Bax/Bak form pores → cytochrome c released.
Cytochrome c + Apaf-1 → apoptosome → activates the caspase cascade (common end-point of both pathways).
Cancer cells survive partly by blocking apoptosis – a target for therapy.

videos.title: Apoptosis (2006) by Drew Berry
summary: No narration (sound design only). Molecular animation of Fas-mediated (extrinsic) apoptosis, published in Sci. STKE 2007.
A killer cell's Fas ligand engages Fas death receptors on the target cell surface, clustering them.
Receptor clustering recruits adaptor proteins (FADD) and initiator caspases inside the cell → caspase cascade.
Executioner caspases dismantle the cell: cytoskeleton collapse, membrane blebbing, nuclear/DNA fragmentation, break-up into apoptotic bodies.

videos.title: Mitosis in an Animal Cell Under the Microscope
summary: 31-s real time-lapse of a Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cell dividing (no narration).
Cell rounds up from the substrate → prophase (chromosomes condense) → metaphase (align at plate) → anaphase (sisters separate) → telophase.
Cytokinesis pinches the cell in two; the daughter cells flatten and re-attach to the dish.
Note: although the slide is titled for apoptosis detection, this clip shows normal mitosis – useful for contrasting the orderly division with apoptotic blebbing/shrinkage.

videos.title: Chromosome – 3D animation (Short)
summary: 14-s 3D animation zooming from a chromosome down to the DNA double helix (no narration).
Reinforces packaging: DNA → nucleosomes → chromatin fibre → condensed chromosome.
Links to the slide: after S phase each chromosome has two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere (G2), versus a single chromatid in G1.

videos.title: GFP mitosis (Short)
summary: 9-s fluorescence time-lapse of a dividing cell with GFP-labelled chromosomes/spindle (no narration).
Chromosomes condense, line up at the metaphase plate, then split to opposite poles (anaphase) and decondense as two nuclei form.
Shows that GFP tagging lets mitosis be followed in living cells in real time.

videos.title: Kinetochore and Mitosis (2014) – Drew Berry
summary: Mitotic chromosome = two identical sister chromatids; spindle microtubules attach from either side.
Kinetochore (red) = interface between chromosome and microtubule ends – one of the largest molecular machines in the cell.

Three jobs: (1) grips dynamic microtubule ends to move the chromosome, (2) senses tension to check correct bi-orientation, (3) broadcasts a 'stop/wait' signal (spindle checkpoint) until attachment is correct.
Once tension is right, dynein motors walk the stop-signal proteins away down the microtubule; kinesins also transport cargo along the spindle.
When every kinetochore is satisfied → anaphase: sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles.

videos.title: Mitosis annotated
summary: Real time-lapse microscopy of a dividing cell (Jeremy Pickett-Heaps) with Drew Berry's animated overlay labelling the structures.
Follow the overlay: spindle poles and microtubules, chromosomes aligning at metaphase, separating in anaphase.
Ends with telophase/cytokinesis – nuclear envelopes re-form and the cell splits into two daughters.

videos.title: See a Salamander Grow From a Single Cell (time-lapse)
summary: 6-min time-lapse of an alpine newt/salamander from fertilised egg to hatching (music only).
Cleavage: the single zygote divides 2 → 4 → 8 … into many smaller cells (blastula).
Gastrulation: cells move inward through the blastopore, forming germ layers.
Neurulation: neural folds rise and close into the neural tube; body axis, somites, eyes, gills and a beating heart then form.
Shows the slide's point: one totipotent cell → many specialised cell types through division + differentiation.

videos.title: Heart cells derived from iPSCs beat in a culture dish
summary: Human skin fibroblasts were reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).
The iPSCs were then differentiated into cardiomyocytes.
The cells contract spontaneously in vitro, with a wave of beating spreading across the dish – evidence that they are functional heart cells.

videos.title: XYClone stem cell laser: ICM excision
summary: Microscope footage of a blastocyst (no narration).
A laser is used to cut out the inner cell mass (ICM) from the surrounding trophectoderm.
The isolated ICM is the source of pluripotent embryonic stem (ES) cells when cultured.
Remember: ICM → embryo proper (pluripotent); trophectoderm → placenta/extra-embryonic tissue.

videos.title: Spemann–Mangold organizer and embryonic induction
summary: Spemann & Mangold (1924) showed that interactions between cell groups pattern the embryo.
The organizer = tissue at the dorsal lip of the blastopore in the gastrulating amphibian (Xenopus) embryo.
Experiment: dorsal-lip tissue is cut from one embryo and grafted into the ventral side of another.
Two days later the host forms a second body axis (conjoined twins) with its own nervous system, eyes and somites.
Conclusion: the organizer induces neighbouring host cells to change fate – embryonic induction.

videos.title: Neutrophil Chemotaxis
summary: Human blood neutrophils migrate rapidly to sites of injury/infection.
They follow chemoattractants released by immune cells or microbes.
In the experiment a micropipette releases chemoattractant; neutrophils polarise and crawl toward it.
When the pipette is moved, the cell immediately sends out a new leading-edge protrusion and reorients – chemotaxis follows the gradient in real time.

videos.title: Crawling neutrophil chasing a bacterium
summary: Classic 1950s 16-mm film: a neutrophil among red blood cells chases a bacterium (no narration).
The neutrophil follows the bacterium's every turn (chemotaxis toward bacterial products).
It finally engulfs the bacterium by phagocytosis – the first step before intracellular killing.

videos.title: Toll-like receptor 4 signalling
videos.note: Heads-up: the slide is titled for NK-cell killing, but this video is actually about TLR4/LPS signalling in innate immunity.
summary: Innate immunity: pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs) detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Humans have 10 TLRs.
TLR4 on macrophages detects LPS from the cell wall of Gram-negative bacteria.
LPS-binding protein carries LPS → CD14 → loads it onto TLR4 with accessory protein MD-2 → TLR4 dimerises.
Dimerised TIR domains recruit the adaptor MyD88 → signalling cascade.
IκB is phosphorylated and degraded → NF-κB freed → enters nucleus → transcription of cytokines and chemokines → inflammation.
Balance matters: too little inflammation → infection; too much → damage from the immune response itself.

videos.title: Immunology in the skin
videos.note: The slide says watch up to 4:32.
summary: Skin = epidermis (keratinocytes; dead corneocytes form the barrier) + dermis (fibroblasts, collagen/elastin, blood and lymph vessels) + fat; commensal microbes help protection.
Sentinels: Langerhans cells (epidermal dendritic cells) and dermal dendritic cells sample antigen.
Effectors: skin holds >2× the T cells in blood, mostly memory. Epidermis → resident CD8 (cytotoxic) T cells; dermis → mostly CD4 helper T cells, plus NK cells, eosinophils, mast cells.
Damage/infection is sensed via PRRs; keratinocytes make antimicrobial peptides, IL-1 and chemokines that recruit neutrophils, macrophages and T cells.
Dendritic cells migrate to lymph nodes and prime naive T cells; effector cytotoxic T cells return and kill virus-infected keratinocytes; memory CD8 T cells then stay in the epidermis.

videos.title: Cytotoxic T cells
summary: Most T cells are naive and circulate through blood, lymph and lymph nodes; naive CD8⁺ T cells can become cytotoxic.
T cells can't see pathogens directly – antigen-presenting cells bring virus peptides on MHC to the lymph node.
A T cell whose unique TCR fits the peptide–MHC complex binds it; co-receptor CD8 also binds; receptors cluster → activation.
The activated cell proliferates into clones that acquire cytotoxic granules (clonal expansion).
Chemical cues guide them to the infection; they recognise the same peptide–MHC on infected cells.
Granule contents (perforin, granzymes) are delivered into the infected cell → it dies. Only infected cells display the peptide, so healthy cells are spared.
